title: First Light
tagline: One storm night at a lighthouse, a ferry that shouldn't cross, and a case nobody wants found.

lamp.text:
The last turn of the stair comes out into glass and wind. The lamp room is colder than the tower below it: a brass lamp the size of a barrel, a lens of cut prisms around it, and beyond the panes the strait going the colour of slate. Your bag is still on your shoulder.

Ysolde Carrow stands at the lamp with a wick in her fist. She does not turn around.

[Ysolde: neutral] "You're late. The wick's wet." She wrings it, and oil and water run between her fingers onto the brass. "The Board sends me a letter and a child, in that order. Put the bag down somewhere it won't roll."

The clockwork under the lamp ticks, unwound. Far out on the water, where no boat should be, there is a point of light.

choices.text: Offer to climb up and check the lens and the burner
choices.say: *I drop the bag against the wall and look up at the lens.* "Let me climb up and look at the lens and the burner. Fresh eyes."

choices.text: Ask why the light matters so much tonight
choices.say: "Why does the light matter so much tonight? More than other nights, I mean."

choices.text: Say nothing, and look out at the water
choices.say: *I say nothing. I set the bag down and go to the glass, and look out at the water.*

why.text:
[Ysolde: angry] "It matters every night." She says it to the lamp, not to you. Then, because you are still standing there: "The glass is falling. North-westerly by full dark. And my nephew, who has more sense than this, is taking the Ketch back across the strait tonight with a passenger who paid him to."

She looks at you for the first time. Pale eyes, wind-burnt skin, a scar across the back of the hand that holds the wick.

[Ysolde: worried] "If this lamp is dark when he's on the Teeth, that's the end of the Reddys on this coast. So. The lens."

sea.text:
You go to the glass. The wind finds the gaps in the frames and hums in them. Below, the cliff, the landing, the shingle, the black line of the Teeth showing as the tide drops.

And out on the water, a light. Not the jetty's; that is behind you, on the lee side. This one sits out in the strait a mile off, low, steady, and when you have watched it for the space of three breaths it goes out, and comes back.

[Ysolde: neutral] "There's nothing out there," she says, without looking. "Fishermen don't cross in this. Lens."

The light stays.

lens.text:
You climb the three iron steps to the lens and put your face to the glass. The prisms throw your own eye back at you a dozen times. One of them, low on the seaward side, has a crack through it like a hair, and the oil cup under the burner has a film of water on it. The wick, when Ysolde threads it, drinks the water first.

She strikes a lucifer. The flame touches the wick, hisses, and dies.

[Ysolde: worried] "Store roof," she says, to no one. "A month of rain into the oil." A second match. The same hiss. The strait outside is a shade darker than it was.

choices.text: Shield the burner with your coat and try a third match
choices.say: *I pull my coat off and hold it open around the burner against the draught.* "Try one more. I'll keep the wind off it."

choices.text: Go down to the kitchen for dry wicks and a clean cup of oil
choices.say: "There'll be dry wicks below? I'll fetch them, and a clean cup of oil." *I take the stair down two at a time.*

kitchen.text:
A hundred and twelve stairs down inside the tower and the kitchen is warm, the range glowing, oilskins dripping by the door. The dry wicks are in a tin on the shelf beside the keeper's log, where she said.

A man is sitting at the table. He has a long black coat and thin gloves and a leather case in his lap, and he was not on the stairs when you came down them.

[Aurel: happy] "The new assistant. Vance, Lighthouse Board." He does not stand. "Mrs Carrow didn't mention me, I expect. She mentions very little. The lamp's not lit."

It is not a question.

choices.text: Ask him how he got into the kitchen
choices.say: *I stop in the doorway with the tin of wicks in my hand.* "How did you get into the kitchen? I didn't pass you on the stairs."

choices.text: Take the wicks and the oil and go straight back up
choices.say: *I take the wicks and a clean cup of oil off the shelf without a word and head straight back up the tower.*

aurel.text:
[Aurel: happy] "Up the stairs from the landing, the same as anyone. The ferryman let me off to stretch my legs before the crossing." He turns the case a quarter turn on his knee. "A hundred and twelve steps. I counted. One wonders how a woman of her years manages them in the dark."

He looks at you with a kind of pleasant patience, as though you were a sum he was close to finishing.

[Aurel: neutral] "Tell me, Hale. What is she like? Does she keep the log every night? Does she ever miss one?"

The wind leans on the door. You have the wicks in your hand and no reason to answer.

lit.text:
The third match takes. The flame runs along the wick, thinks about it, and stands up yellow and steady. Ysolde drops the glass over it, winds the clockwork with both hands, and the lens begins to turn: a slow bar of light sweeps out across the rain and the black water, and the room fills with the tick.

[Ysolde: determined] "Right." It is the nearest thing to thanks you are going to hear.

Then, from far below, a brass whistle: two blasts, a gap, two more. Ysolde's head comes up.

[Ysolde: worried] "That's Tam. That's the landing, not the jetty." She is already at the stair. "Something's in the water."

choices.text: Run down the landing stairs after her
choices.say: *I take the stair after her, two steps at a time, out into the rain and down towards the landing.*

choices.text: Stay with the lamp and keep it burning; let her go
choices.say: "Go. I'll keep it burning." *I stay by the lamp and put my hand on the clockwork's crank.*

stairs.text:
A hundred and twelve steps in the rain with a rope rail and the beam going over your head every eight seconds. Tam Reddy is at the bottom, soaked, the whistle still in his teeth, his lantern held out over the black water as if it could pull something back.

[Tam: worried] "Something went over the side." He says it before you've reached him. "I'd the Ketch at the jetty with her head to the wind, waiting on my passenger, and I hear it hit the water off the point. Here. Not there." He points along the shore. "And the passenger's gone off her. Coat, case, gone."

Ysolde comes down the last steps behind you without a word and takes the lantern out of his hand.

choices.text: Take the lantern and go out along the shore to look
choices.say: *I take the lantern from Ysolde and start out along the shingle, holding it low over the wrack.* "Stay where I can see you both."

choices.text: Tell Tam to get the Ketch's lamps lit, and go with Ysolde
choices.say: "Tam, get the Ketch's lamps lit, every one, so she can be seen from the water." *I turn to follow Ysolde along the shore.*

stay.text:
Her boots go down the stair and the room is yours: the tick, the rain on the glass, the bar of light going round. You wind the clockwork when it slackens, the way she did, and watch the strait.

The light out on the water is still there. As the beam passes over it, it blinks: three short, one long, three short. Then again. Then it goes out and does not come back.

Below, a long time later, a brass whistle: two blasts, a gap, two more. Then boots on the outside stair and Tam Reddy's voice calling your name up the tower, hoarse with rain.

shore.text:
The shingle gives under your boots. The beam comes round every eight seconds and shows you the shore in slices: weed, a spar, a dead gull, weed. Tam is counting the Teeth under his breath as the tide uncovers them.

The third sweep shows you a leather case lying in the wrack, its strap snapped, water running out of the seams. Ysolde gets to it first and does not pick it up.

[Tam: surprised] "That's his. That's the Board man's."

[Aurel: neutral] "It is." He is standing on the rocks above you with no lantern at all, hat gone, coat black with rain, perfectly calm. "I slipped on your stairs, Mrs Carrow, and it went in. I'd be grateful for it back. The Board's papers are in it. Nothing that would interest anyone here."

Ysolde has not moved. Her hand with the scar on it is a fist.

choices.text: Pick up the case and hand it to him
choices.say: *I pick the case up out of the weed, water running from its seams, and hold it out to him.* "Here. Your papers."

choices.text: Pick up the case and give it to Ysolde instead
choices.say: *I pick the case up out of the weed and put it into Ysolde's hands instead of his.* "The keeper's light, the keeper's shore. She decides."

choices.text: Turn the lantern to the strait and signal the light you saw
choices.say: *I turn my back on him, lift the lantern towards the strait and open and close its shutter: three short, one long, three short, the way the light out there did.*

shore_late.text:
By the time you reach the shore the rain has eased to something you can see through. Tam is alone on the shingle with his lantern and a leather case at his feet, its strap snapped, water running out of the seams.

[Tam: sad] "He went off the stairs. The Board man. Aunt Ysolde went down after him with the lantern and I've not seen either of them since." He wipes his face with a wet sleeve, which does nothing. "That's his case. I'm not touching it. I was paid to carry him, not to go through his things."

Out on the strait the light you watched is gone. The Teeth are showing, a black line in the beam.

choices.text: Open the case here, in the lantern light
choices.say: *I kneel on the shingle and work the wet straps loose in the lantern light.* "If it's only the Board's papers, no harm done."

choices.text: Leave it for the tide; it isn't yours
choices.say: "Leave it. It isn't ours, and the tide will have it in an hour." *I turn back towards the stairs.*

chapel.text:
The chapel has no roof but it has walls, and that is enough. Ysolde sets the lantern on the altar stone, cuts the case's wet straps with a knife from her boot, and lifts out a packet of letters wrapped in oilcloth, the seals still whole. She knows the hand on the outside. You can see her know it.

She reads standing, the lantern between you, the rain coming through the empty bell arch. It takes a long time. When she is done she folds the top sheet along its old creases.

[Ysolde: sad] "Edwin wrote these the week he died. To the Board." Her voice is quite steady. "They name the Pryces. What they paid him to put the light out for, and which nights, and that he'd stopped. He posted them from Caulder on the Tuesday. He went off the stairs on the Thursday." She looks at the bell arch. "Pryce sits on the Board now. That man came to burn these, and to see what I'd cost."

She holds the packet out over the lantern flame. Not into it. Over it.

[Ysolde: determined] "Your post, Hale. Your log, after tonight. What goes in it?"

choices.text: Tell her to burn them: the strait has taken enough from her
choices.say: "Burn them." *I say it quietly.* "The strait has taken enough from you. Let it have the Pryces' secret too."

choices.text: Take the letters from her hand and say they go to the magistrate at Caulder on the morning ferry
choices.say: *I take the packet out of her hand before the flame can reach it.* "These go to the magistrate at Caulder on the morning ferry. In the log: letters recovered from the shore."

end_lost.text:
The case is heavier than it looks. He takes it from you with both gloved hands and inclines his head, the way a man does when a waiter has got something right.

[Aurel: happy] "Obliged. The Board will hear that the new man has sense." To Ysolde, more quietly: "And that the light was lit, Mrs Carrow. On time. I'll say so."

He goes up the landing stairs without a lantern and does not slip. Tam looks at Ysolde, and Ysolde looks at the strait, and nobody says anything until the Ketch's whistle sounds from the jetty an hour later and the ferry goes out across the Teeth with its lamps lit and comes safe to the far side.

In the morning the keeper's log reads, in Ysolde's hand: *Lamp lit at 6.40, late. Wick wet. Assistant keeper arrived. Nothing seen.* She does not speak to you for a week. Then she teaches you the clockwork.

end_signal.text:
You turn the lantern out to the strait and open and close the shutter: three short, one long, three short, the pattern the light made. You don't know what it means. You know that someone out there does.

The light out on the water comes back, once, long, and then there is the sound of an engine on the wind, going away.

[Aurel: angry] "That was unwise." It is the first thing he has said with any feeling in it. He comes down off the rocks, takes the case out of the wrack himself, and walks past Ysolde to the stairs. She lets him. Her eyes are on the strait.

[Ysolde: surprised] "Eleven years," she says, "and nobody ever signalled them back." Then, to Tam: "The Ketch stays at the jetty tonight. Whatever he paid you."

[Tam: surprised] "He paid me plenty."

[Ysolde: determined] "Then you've had a good night."

The beam goes round over all three of you, eight seconds, eight seconds, and the Teeth stay dark, and nothing crosses the strait until first light.

end_quiet.text:
You leave it where it lies. The tide is making; in an hour the wrack line will be under water and the case with it, and the strait will have whatever was in it, as it has had everything else.

Tam says nothing, which for Tam is a speech. You walk back along the shingle together with the beam going over you.

Ysolde is in the lamp room when you climb back up, dry, winding the clockwork, as if she had never left it. The passenger is not mentioned. In the morning the Ketch crosses in a flat calm with no one aboard but Tam, and the log reads: *Lamp lit at 6.40. Wick wet. Assistant keeper arrived.*

Some nights, for years, you will see a light out on the strait where no boat should be. You will keep the lamp lit. That is the job.

end_ash.text:
She does not thank you. She lowers the packet into the flame and holds it there with the burnt hand until the oilcloth catches, and then she lays it on the altar stone and the two of you watch Edwin Carrow's handwriting go brown and black and up through the bell arch into the rain.

[Ysolde: sad] "He'd have wanted them read." The last sheet curls. "He always did want things read."

Vance is gone by morning; Tam swears he never came back aboard, and the Ketch crosses without him. The Board writes in the spring to say the inspector found the light well kept. Ysolde writes back once.

You keep the lamp with her, winter and summer. She never says Edwin's name again, and the light at Harrow Point is never dark, not for one hour, not for anyone.

end_truth.text:
The oilcloth is warm from the flame. She lets you take it. For a moment her hand stays where it was, open over the lantern, and then she closes it.

[Ysolde: determined] "Caulder magistrate's a Pryce cousin."

"Then the one after him," you say, or something like it. "Or the newspaper. Or the Board, with your name on the covering letter and mine under it."

Tam has come into the chapel behind you, dripping, and heard the end of it.

[Tam: determined] "Ketch crosses at first light," he says. "Flat calm or not. And I'm not carrying any passengers but you."

The lamp goes round over the roofless walls, eight seconds, eight seconds. Somewhere on the stairs, or the shore, or the strait, Aurel Vance is working out what the three of you cost, and finding, for once, that he hasn't the money.

In the morning the keeper's log reads, in a new hand: *Lamp lit at 6.40. Letters recovered from the shore, carried to Caulder. Light kept.*
